clue.text: eg Is this suitable for the fire?

definitions.text: eg Is this suitable for the fire?

blocks.clueFragment: Is this suitable for the fire?
blocks.note: surface reading: someone wondering whether a log or scrap of paper may be thrown on the fire
setter's reading: the question itself is offered as an example of a pressing issue that is literally about burning

explanation.surface: Someone holds up a piece of junk and asks whether it can go on the fire.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'eg' tells you the quoted question is a specimen of the answer: a question about burning, which the idiom recasts as an urgent, much-debated issue.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names a pressing matter everyone wants settled, and here the example is quite literally about whether something will burn.

clue.text: Bet the gallery will do this

definitions.text: Bet the gallery will do this

blocks.note: a spec is short for a speculation, a gamble or bet
the Tate is the famous London art gallery

explanation.surface: A confident wager that the people in the gallery seats will simply watch.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue does double duty: a gallery here is also the audience in the cheap seats of a theatre, and what an audience does is watch.
explanation.definitionFit: Spectators in a theatre gallery or at a golf course look on rather than take part, so watching is exactly their role.

clue.text: Language from overseas

indicators.note: the answer is taken out of the following word, lifted straight from inside its letters

blocks.note: the second to fifth letters of this word

explanation.surface: A foreign tongue picked up somewhere abroad.
explanation.definitionFit: Erse is an old name for the Gaelic tongue of Scotland or Ireland, so it is a language.

clue.text: Had meal about 1st April and started enterprise

indicators.note: first tells us to keep only the opening letter of the month named next to it
about means going around, so the meal word is wrapped around the single letter

blocks.note: to have a midday meal is to have lunched
the first letter of the month

explanation.surface: Someone ate lunch on April Fools' Day and then set up a new business.
explanation.definitionFit: To launch something is to set a new venture going, so launched means started an enterprise.

clue.text: Notice the narrow opening at sea

blocks.note: an ad, an advertisement, is a public notice
a rift is a crack or narrow gap

explanation.surface: Spotting a thin gap in the hull while out on the ocean.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At sea' seems to set the scene for the narrow opening, but it is the definition in its figurative sense of lost or confused.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases describe drifting without direction, whether a boat literally or a person figuratively bewildered.

clue.text: High-flier's a stimulus to the plant

blocks.note: the skylark is a bird famous for soaring high while singing
a spur is an incentive or stimulus

explanation.surface: An ambitious high achiever is spurring on some plant, perhaps a factory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plant' could be an industrial site the high-flier runs, but it is a garden flower.
explanation.definitionFit: Larkspur is a tall garden flower, a kind of delphinium, so it is a plant.

clue.text: Delivery address

blocks.note: first meaning: one's manner of speaking, as in a clear delivery
second meaning: a formal talk given to an audience

explanation.walkthrough: Read together the words suggest a postal destination; each is in fact a sense of a spoken word.
explanation.definitionFit: The word covers both a person's way of talking and a formal talk given to listeners.

clue.text: Fit with padding to make plump

blocks.note: fit as in healthy
furniture given padding and covers has been upholstered

explanation.surface: Stuffing cushions to make them nicely rounded.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fit' seems to be the verb for fitting padding; it is the adjective for being in good health.
explanation.definitionFit: Describing a person as nicely padded like a sofa is a humorous idiom for being on the fat side.

clue.text: Superior worker's advantage

blocks.note: upper means higher or superior
a hand is a manual worker, as in farmhand

explanation.surface: A senior worker enjoys a benefit over the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Having the dominant position in a contest is an idiom for holding the advantage.

clue.text: Bulky specimen needing no introduction

indicators.note: with no introduction the word loses its opening letter

blocks.note: a sample is a specimen

explanation.surface: A large example so famous it needs no introduction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Needing no introduction' sounds like praise for a celebrity; it tells you to drop the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Ample means large or generous in size, close to the sense of bulky.

clue.text: p or n? (non-clue, possibly)

indicators.note: possibly suggests these letters could form something else if rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written, hyphen ignored

explanation.surface: A setter sheepishly offers two bare letters, admitting it is hardly a clue at all.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracket pretends to apologise for a clue that is barely a clue; p and n are the physics symbols for proton and neutron.
explanation.definitionFit: Protons and neutrons are the two particles making up an atomic nucleus, collectively called by this name.

clue.text: There's material for a writer in it

definitions.text: There's material for a writer in it

blocks.clueFragment: There's material for a writer in it
blocks.note: surface reading: some event or story would make good subject matter for an author
setter's reading: the material is the fluid a pen is dipped in, held in a little pot on a desk

explanation.surface: Someone remarks that a juicy story would make a good book.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the small container set into an old school desk holding the liquid a writer dips a pen into.

clue.text: Cattle without water

blocks.note: first meaning: an old word for oxen or cows, as in neatherd
second meaning: of a spirit, served undiluted

explanation.walkthrough: Together it reads like livestock in a drought; the cattle sense is archaic but common in crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both an old collective term for bovine animals and the barman's term for whisky served straight.

clue.text: Stop work and say nothing at society dance

blocks.note: to shut up is to stop talking
S is the abbreviation for society
a hop is an informal dance

explanation.surface: Someone downs tools and stays silent at a smart society ball.
explanation.definitionFit: To close the shop for the day is an idiom for ceasing business or giving up working.

clue.text: Quire being delivered to editor is questioned

indicators.note: delivered in the sense of set free, so these letters are released from their order

blocks.note: taken as written
ED is the standard abbreviation for editor

explanation.surface: A batch of paper sent to the editor's office raises some queries.
explanation.walkthrough: A quire is a set of 24 or 25 sheets of paper, which makes the delivery to an editor sound natural.
explanation.definitionFit: To query something is to ask about it, so queried and questioned are synonyms.

clue.text: Fresh in part of the Channel?

blocks.note: taken as written
the Solent is the strait between the Isle of Wight and mainland England, an arm of the English Channel

explanation.surface: Asking whether some new thing is found in a stretch of the English Channel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fresh' looks like an adjective for water; it is the informal sense of cheeky.
explanation.definitionFit: Fresh can mean cheeky or impudent, as in getting fresh with someone, which matches rudely disrespectful.

clue.text: One officer after drink getting the classical cover

indicators.note: after tells us the officer pieces come behind the drink in the order of letters

blocks.note: port is a fortified wine
I is the Roman numeral for one
CO stands for commanding officer

explanation.surface: An army officer after a glass of something gets classical cover, perhaps from a defending lawyer.
explanation.definitionFit: A colonnaded porch at the entrance of a building in Greek or Roman style provides a roofed shelter.

clue.text: Excess pother travelling with a learner

indicators.note: things travelling are on the move, so these letters move from where they stand

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
L is for learner, as on a learner driver's plate

explanation.surface: Too much fuss on the road with a learner driver at the wheel.
explanation.walkthrough: Pother is an old word for a fuss or commotion.
explanation.definitionFit: A plethora is an overabundance, far more of something than is needed, matching excess.

clue.text: Arctic explorer could be drug-limited

definitions.note: a phrase describing the explorer's condition; the answer is an adjective

blocks.note: ice is slang for crystal methamphetamine
bound means confined or restricted

explanation.surface: A polar explorer might be hemmed in by drug laws.
explanation.definitionFit: A ship or traveller trapped in frozen polar seas is held fast by the ice, a fate an Arctic expedition risks.

clue.text: English trees stay around in an affluent state

indicators.note: around suggests letters scattered about, so they are rearranged

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for English
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: English trees remain standing in a wealthy nation.
explanation.definitionFit: Living on this street is an idiom for a comfortable, prosperous life free of money worries.

clue.text: Joint fixer

blocks.note: surface reading: an orthopaedic surgeon or someone who mends a creaking knee or hip
setter's reading: a joint of meat, held together on a long metal pin for roasting

explanation.walkthrough: 'Joint' suggests the body or carpentry; here it is a piece of meat for the oven.
explanation.definitionFit: This long pin pierces chunks of meat to hold them in place while they cook.

clue.text: Lascar abroad could be a rogue

indicators.note: abroad means scattered widely, so these letters are spread into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written; a lascar is a sailor from India or Southeast Asia

explanation.surface: A foreign sailor overseas might turn out to be a villain.
explanation.walkthrough: A lascar is an Indian or Southeast Asian sailor. The published grid printed RASCAE, a misprint for the word the anagram gives.
explanation.definitionFit: A rascal is a dishonest or mischievous person, a synonym for a scoundrel.

clue.text: A river guy, they say

indicators.note: they say points to how a word is spoken rather than written

blocks.note: to guy someone is to mock or rib them

explanation.surface: Someone reports a river named after a man.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tees is a river in north-east England.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the name of a river running through Teesside in the north-east of England.

clue.text: Screen right round American island

indicators.note: turned round means facing the opposite way, so the abbreviation is read backwards

blocks.note: RT is an abbreviation for right
Ellis Island in New York harbour was the immigration station

explanation.surface: A screen set up right around an island in America.
explanation.definitionFit: A lattice of wooden strips, often for climbing plants, can serve as a garden partition or screen.

clue.text: Stylish swipe that gives body support

blocks.note: hip means fashionable
bone is slang for steal

explanation.surface: A smart sweep of the arm that props a person up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swipe' seems to be a blow or swing; it is the slang sense of steal, as is bone.
explanation.definitionFit: The pelvic bones form part of the skeleton bearing the trunk's weight, a structural support of the body.

clue.text: Buttons, perhaps silver, appearing in drill

indicators.note: appearing in places the metal symbol inside the abbreviation for drill

blocks.note: PE is physical education, the school exercise once called drill
Ag is the chemical symbol for silver

explanation.surface: Buttons, maybe silver ones, turning up on army drill uniform.
explanation.walkthrough: Buttons is the stock name for a pageboy in a hotel or great house, from his buttoned uniform; Buttons is also the servant in the pantomime Cinderella.
explanation.definitionFit: A boy servant or bellhop in a hotel was nicknamed Buttons for his livery, so he is an example of this.

clue.text: Canoe capsized in the water

indicators.note: a boat that has capsized is overturned and jumbled, so its letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A canoe has overturned, tipping its paddler into the water.
explanation.definitionFit: The sea is often called simply the water, and this word names the open sea.

clue.text: Airs produced when playing organ with care

indicators.note: playing suggests letters at play, moving freely into another order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Melodies come out when an organist plays carefully.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Airs' looks like tunes from the organ; it means putting on airs, a haughty manner.
explanation.definitionFit: Putting on airs means behaving superiorly, so airs is a fair plural noun for haughty pride.
